For a space elevator to work, the end of the cable in space would need to be AT LEAST way out at ~35K km in geostationary orbit, right?

Cuz the point in space would need to be stationary relative to the point on the ground. A geostationary end point would, in theory, produce zero outward centrifugal force. But as the orbital endpoint is extended beyond geostationary orbit, centrifugal forces would begin to express and create negative tension on the cable.

And if used as an elevator, the craft that goes up the cable would need to detach from the endpoint and then get to an orbit that doesn’t require fuel-burn to maintain.

Detaching the craft before reaching the cable endpoint would be simple at the geostationary orbit. Just detach and float. No fuel needed to maintain orbit.

Detaching before geostationary orbit will require fuel-burn to speed up, since the craft wouldn’t already be moving fast enough to maintain orbit.

Detaching past the geostationary point would also require fuel-burn, but to slow down. Without burn, the craft would sling outward into higher orbits.

Thinking out loud a bit. Never thought all the way through some of the math involved to pragmatically use a space elevator.

There’s some calculus involved to figure out just how far the endpoint needs to be in order to reach the zero-tension point.

The weight of the cable at lower altitudes will pull the whole thing down. But the cable gets lighter to the point of weightlessness at higher altitudes. A certain amount of centrifugal force will be necessary to counter the effect of gravity on the lower segments. The mass of the endpoint factors in as well.

But once you’ve figured out where the zero-tension altitude is for a given cable and endpoint system - which will certainly be beyond the ~35K km geostationary orbit - you can achieve weightlessness in the endpoint.

Pushing the endpoint farther out past the zero-tension altitude will then: 1) begin to increase negative cable tension as a function of increasing centrifugal force 2) keep the cable/endpoint + payload from falling 3) and at some point, create negative gravity in the endpoint.

If you get it far enough out to create -1G of gravity, a space tourist could stand on the “ceiling” of the endpoint with the same feeling of gravity while standing on Earth. Yet if that tourist were to look directly above them in that position, they’d be looking “down” at Earth.
